content: Various types of vaccines have been developed to combat the SARS-CoV-2 virus and the resulting COVID-19 disease. These vaccines are now widely used across the globe. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of COVID-19 vaccines, whether as part of a full primary vaccination series or as booster doses, in preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, the COVID-19 L·OVE platform, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, regulatory agency websites, and Retraction Watch. The last search was performed on November 5, 2021. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared COVID-19 vaccines to placebo, no vaccine, other active vaccines, or alternative vaccine schedules. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence for all outcomes except immunogenicity. Data for each vaccine were synthesized separately, and summary effect estimates were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The analysis included 41 RCTs evaluating 12 different vaccines, encompassing both homologous and heterologous vaccine schedules as well as the effects of booster doses. Among these, 32 trials were multicenter studies, and five were multinational. The sample sizes of the trials ranged from 60 to 44,325 participants. Most trials included participants aged 18 years or older, with some trials including younger age groups (12–17 years or 3–17 years). Twenty-nine trials provided data on individuals aged over 60 years, and three trials included immunocompromised patients. However, no trials included pregnant women. The follow-up periods varied, with 16 trials having a follow-up of two months or less, 20 trials with two to six months, and five trials with six to 12 months. Eighteen reports were based on preplanned interim analyses. The overall risk of bias was low for all outcomes in eight RCTs, while 33 trials raised concerns for at least one outcome. Additionally, 343 registered RCTs had results that were not yet available at the time of this review. The study focused on critical outcomes, including confirmed symptomatic COVID-19, severe or critical COVID-19, and serious adverse events (SAEs), specifically for the 10 vaccines approved by the World Health Organization (WHO). For other outcomes and vaccines, the main text of the review provides further details. Confirmed Symptomatic COVID-19 High-certainty evidence demonstrated that several vaccines significantly reduce the incidence of symptomatic COVID-19 compared to placebo. These vaccines include: BNT162b2 (BioNTech/Pfizer): Vaccine efficacy (VE) of 97.84% (95% CI: 44.25% to 99.92%; 2 RCTs, 44,077 participants). mRNA-1273 (Moderna): VE of 93.20% (95% CI: 91.06% to 94.83%; 2 RCTs, 31,632 participants). ChAdOx1 (Oxford/AstraZeneca): VE of 70.23% (95% CI: 62.10% to 76.62%; 2 RCTs, 43,390 participants). Ad26.COV2.S (Janssen): VE of 66.90% (95% CI: 59.10% to 73.40%; 1 RCT, 39,058 participants). BBIBP-CorV (Sinopharm): VE of 78.10% (95% CI: 64.80% to 86.30%; 1 RCT, 25,463 participants). BBV152 (Bharat Biotech): VE of 77.80% (95% CI: 65.20% to 86.40%; 1 RCT, 16,973 participants). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that NVX-CoV2373 (Novavax) likely reduces symptomatic COVID-19 (VE of 82.91%; 95% CI: 50.49% to 94.10%; 3 RCTs, 42,175 participants). For CoronaVac (Sinovac), low-certainty evidence indicated a VE of 69.81% (95% CI: 12.27% to 89.61%; 2 RCTs, 19,852 participants). Severe or Critical COVID-19 High-certainty evidence showed that several vaccines substantially reduce the incidence of severe or critical COVID-19 compared to placebo: BNT162b2: VE of 95.70% (95% CI: 73.90% to 99.90%; 1 RCT, 46,077 participants). mRNA-1273: VE of 98.20% (95% CI: 92.80% to 99.60%; 1 RCT, 28,451 participants). Ad26.COV2.S: VE of 76.30% (95% CI: 57.90% to 87.50%; 1 RCT, 39,058 participants). BBV152: VE of 93.40% (95% CI: 57.10% to 99.80%; 1 RCT, 16,976 participants). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that NVX-CoV2373 likely reduces severe or critical COVID-19 (VE of 100.00%; 95% CI: 86.99% to 100.00%; 1 RCT, 25,452 participants). Two trials reported high efficacy for CoronaVac in preventing severe or critical disease, but the results had wide confidence intervals and could not be pooled. Serious Adverse Events (SAEs) The evidence indicated that some vaccines likely result in little to no difference in the risk of serious adverse events compared to placebo: mRNA-1273: Risk ratio (RR) of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.78 to 1.08; 2 RCTs, 34,072 participants). ChAdOx1 (Oxford/AstraZeneca): RR of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.72 to 1.07; 7 RCTs, 58,182 participants). Ad26.COV2.S: RR of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.69 to 1.22; 1 RCT, 43,783 participants). BBV152: RR of 0.65 (95% CI: 0.43 to 0.97; 1 RCT, 25,928 participants). For these vaccines, the absolute difference in SAEs was fewer than 5 per 1,000 participants. However, the evidence for SAEs was uncertain for BNT162b2, CoronaVac, BBIBP-CorV, and NVX-CoV2373. Limitations and Implications The study noted that the results cannot be generalized to certain populations, such as pregnant women, individuals with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection, or immunocompromised individuals, due to trial exclusions. Most trials had short follow-up periods and were conducted before the emergence of variants of concern. Future research should focus on the long-term effects of vaccines, comparisons between different vaccines and schedules, efficacy and safety in specific populations, and outcomes such as prevention of long COVID-19. Continuous evaluation of vaccine efficacy against emerging variants remains essential.
